 US and Iran are quietly negotiating as Middle East remains on edge. Here’s what to know
 By Mostafa Salem 
 Updated Nov 9, 2026, 5:06 PM ET 
 PUBLISHED Nov 9, 2026, 12:00 AM ET 
 A member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps at a military training center for ordinary citizens at Tajrish Square in Tehran on November 2. 
 Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters 
 Donald Trump 
 The Middle East

 US President Donald Trump is offering his clearest indication yet that intensified diplomacy could avert another major round of fighting with Iran, in the wake of his party’s disastrous midterm election results.
 Trump told CNN on Sunday that renewed US military attacks are “highly unlikely” if Tehran makes progress toward an agreement on its nuclear program and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. He also told CBS’ “60 Minutes” that he was “not looking to” escalate the war.
 Trump went further Monday after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, saying he does not believe that additional military action against Iran is necessary for now. “At this point, it won’t be necessary, taking the military action,” Trump said during a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room.
 But Trump made clear that the military option remains available if circumstances change. “Should there be any change with respect to developments in the Middle East, the United States of America is fully locked and loaded,” he said. “We don’t think there’ll be any reason to use it,” he added.
 Iran and the United States have quietly been negotiating a sensitive agreement that could avert a return to all-out war and open the door to broader talks.
 But hopes of a deal are being tempered by Washington, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying Sunday that he “wouldn’t say we’re on the verge of a breakthrough.”
 Both sides and Qatar, which is mediating, have revealed little about the discussions, even as diplomatic activity has accelerated since Tuesday’s midterms.
 What’s changed since the midterms?
 The Republican losses in the elections have added another dimension to the negotiations. Vice President JD Vance said afterward that the war was among the reasons Republicans lost both houses of Congress.
 Trump told “60 Minutes” that he did not disagree with Vance’s assessment, acknowledging that voters “didn’t like the war.” But he strongly defended the decision to attack Iran, saying that if he had to make the decision again, his answer would be “an emphatic yes.”

 Iran, meanwhile, has sought to use the election results to press its negotiating position. “American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday.
 Trump continues to project confidence about the US military position, while Iran has repeatedly threatened to expand the war geographically if it is attacked again.
 Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, third left, attends a meeting with high-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey on Tehran on October 26. Flanking him are Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei, second left, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, third right. 
 Iranian Presidency Office/AP 
 What is being discussed?
 Both sides have several key demands that, on paper, are nonstarters for the other.
 Trump seeks to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program, which Tehran sees as a matter of national sovereignty.
 Publicly, Iran is posturing, insisting it will not negotiate with Washington over the program or reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz unless seven preconditions are met — including ending the war on “all fronts” and lifting a maritime blockade. The specifics have yet to be made public.
 Hundreds of kilograms of highly enriched uranium, the fissile material needed to produce a nuclear bomb if further enriched to weapons grade, remain hidden somewhere in Iran. Tehran has used this stockpile as leverage in its talks with the US. Reports indicate that Washington wants the uranium diluted or transferred to another country for safekeeping. It is unclear how far the two sides have progressed on that point.
 Iran has contended that its nuclear program is for generating energy and not military purposes.
 For Iran, aside from not ceding ground on its nuclear program or the Strait of Hormuz, there are key economic goals.
 As one of the world’s largest oil producers, Iran has found it increasingly difficult to sell crude on global markets under US sanctions. Billions of dollars in Iranian assets held in foreign banks also remain frozen. Washington appears to be weighing relief on these restrictions, a move that could help Tehran ease the severe economic strain on its population amid record inflation.
 Iran also wants compensation from the US for the killing of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and his top military commanders in airstrikes at the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February.
 Qatar is mediating between the two sides and circulating a framework document that both Washington and Tehran are amending. The process has been underway for weeks, possibly months, but has intensified in recent days amid fears of fresh strikes.
 Trump met with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, in Washington on Monday. Afterward, Trump said Qatar and other Arab states bordering the Persian Gulf would prefer the “status quo,” and he expressed optimism that the conflict could soon end.
 “We’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon,” Trump said.
 Vessels at the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on October 12. 
 Stringer/Reuters 
 What’s stopping a deal?
 So far, neither side has been willing to budge on its demands.
 Before leaving Sunday for the Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested the two sides remained far from an agreement.
 “Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”
 After successive rounds of open conflict, Tehran’s trust in Washington has almost vanished. Iran has not forgotten that the conflict began while nuclear talks with the US were underway.
 Iran is concerned that relinquishing any leverage could invite the US and Israel to strike again, leaving it exposed and without effective negotiating tools. If Iran is attacked after opening the Strait of Hormuz and relinquishing control over the enriched uranium, it would be left even more exposed and in a weaker negotiating position.
 Trump is balancing his ties with Arab partners and Israel — both of which view the Islamic Republic as a threat — and faces scrutiny if he walks away from the war without a major concession from Iran. Tehran also wants to protect its regional proxies and allies in Lebanon, Iraq and Yemen. Those militias have fought on behalf of the Islamic Republic regionally and are loyal to Tehran, but they have come under existential pressure over the past three years.
 In September, Iran’s ally in Yemen, the Houthi rebels, launched a lightning offensive, capturing another key maritime chokepoint on the Red Sea — the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — and giving Tehran potential influence over an additional waterway. The Houthis have since ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia in response to Riyadh’s military support for the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

 The US wants to deny Iran the capability to build a nuclear weapon, including advanced equipment that could allow it to do so.
 Iran’s Arab neighbors are divided over any agreement that would hand Tehran too much power and cement its desired hegemony. Iran wants to administer the Strait of Hormuz, the maritime corridor through which wealthy Arab states export most of their oil and gas. Control of the waterway would give Tehran decisive influence over what enters and leaves the region. This, too, would go against the demands of the US, which wants to see open waterways and would be loath to hand Iran a key gain from the war.
 Colorful tree and flower decorations remain on the walls of a rubble-strewn classroom at Shajareh Tayyebeh school, in Minab, southern Iran, on September 7. More than 100 people were killed in a US airstrike on Feb. 28, according to Iranian authorities. 
 Vahid Salemi/AP 
 So, will war resume?
 There have been some attacks, but both sides have played them down, a sign perhaps that neither wants to derail talks.
 Some outlets report that talks between the two sides have moved closer to agreement. The New York Times has indicated that Iran is willing to reengage in nuclear negotiations.
 There has been no independent confirmation, but any concessions from Iran on its nuclear program, or even willingness to discuss the topic, would be considered a breakthrough.
 Yet, despite reports of progress, the risk of an all-out war remains real. The US still has a vast military presence in the Middle East that could launch a major assault on Trump’s orders.
 Vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz with oil and gas continue to come under Iranian attack.
 The US is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear program and has launched a task force aimed at blocking Tehran from using land routes to move advanced weapons and other materials — signs that Washington is intensifying pressure rather than easing it.

 Meanwhile, Iranian hard-liners who believe Tehran has already emerged victorious in its war with the US are seizing on Trump’s midterm losses to demand that he pay a steeper price for an exit from the conflict. Should a deal be reached by the more reformist-minded Iranian leaders involved in talks, they could face opposition at home.
 Over the past weeks, Iranian military commanders have stepped up their warnings, claiming that Iran possesses weaponry capable of striking more targets and inflicting even greater damage than before.
 So, even if Trump is willing to reach a deal, it is far from clear whether Iran is ready to accept one.
 CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.
